en: Yogāmbarīsādhanaratnamālā, Matsunami 312 (old no. 230) [I.]:
This is actually a composite codex.
[1] Homage to Yogāmbara!
She, who clings to the glorious body of the Sky-Lord (Viṣṇu), through her state of having shed all impurity, was born with effort for the sake of sprinkling away the afflictions of the earth;
she is purified by the stream of Dharma and stands as a witness to the destruction of dense ignorance.
Having bowed to her who is fierce from the beginning, whose rays are like the moon and sun, and whose roar is most intense;
Having prostrated with the offering of his entire body before Nāgārjuna and the noble Āryavarma—
their feet having been massaged and purified by that merit— he [proceeds].
By me, the jewel of the samādhi of the four seats.
Desiring to set forth for the benefit of the world the jewel-garland of the *Yogāmbarī* sādhana, I compose this work, made beautiful by its arrangement in the charming *cāru* meter.
[This is] a row of stainless jewels consisting of radiant applications.

Here indeed, a yogi consecrated in the great tantra of the Four Seats (Catuḥpīṭha), having sat down facing west upon a soft seat in a meditation chamber adorned with canopies and other ornaments in a location pleasing to the mind, decorated with clean garments and ornaments, happy and with a face full of joy, should perform the purification of the hands and tongue as follows.

In this regard, the procedure is as follows: Having placed a red syllable *A* upon the solar disc on the palm of the right hand, and [the syllables] *ŚUṂ*, *KṢUṂ*, *YUṂ*, *HŪṂ*, and *A* sequentially upon the white and other [colored] rays [of the left hand], one should take hold of them as having the form of single-pointed needles. Then, upon the lunar disc on the palm of the left hand, one places a white syllable *SA* upon the white solar disc; [and the syllables] *SMA*, *RYUṂ*, *HMRYUṂ*, *KṢMRYUṂ*, *YMRYUṂ*, and *SA* upon the yellow and other rays known as one's own [colors]. These should be taken hold of as having the form of lotus petals fashioned from seed-syllables. This is the purification of the hands (*karaviśuddhi*).

Then, having visualized an eight-petaled lotus joined with the syllable *hrīḥ* at the opening of the throat, one should consecrate it with the mantra: *oṃ aḥ jihvāsaṃvartani hūṃ phaṭ*. This is the purification of the tongue. || o ||

Then, having placed the *argha* and *pādya* waters in vessels such as a conch shell and having consecrated them by reciting the respective mantra and mudrā, one should set them down in that same manner. The sequence for this is as follows:
Having firmly formed the vajra-bind, with the words "the smoke of the three impurities is raised," one should bind [it] with the hand attached to the *argha* vessel.
*Oṃ pratīccha arghaṃ hūṃ svāhā*.
Having thus recited this twenty-one times— three times seven— likewise,
having formed the vajra-fist and joined it with the white command,
one should effortlessly cast down Padmā, Śaṅkhā, and Dhūmā.
Having taken a flower with this [mantra]:

*oṃ pravarasatkāraṃ pratīccha hūṃ svāhā*, one should empower it by reciting this aforementioned [mantra] (*vā* or *vārān*) and place it there. This is the procedure for the water-offering (*argha*) and the foot-water (*pādya*).

Furthermore, having placed the common components of worship, such as the offerings for the *balis*, in appropriate vessels, one should perform the double vajra-binding (*vajrabandha*) while touching them with the *siṃhinī-mudrā* joined evenly, reciting: "Oṃ sarvasaṃśodhani hūṃ phaṭ. Having consecrated all the components of worship as before, one should sprinkle them and set them down. This is the procedure for sprinkling the components of worship.

Then, established in the *sattvaparyaṅka* posture with the *samādhi-mudrā*, fixing his gaze on the tip of his nose, he should focus upon the maṇḍala adorned with the body of the deity whose characteristics will be described below in the space before him. He should worship it with the fivefold offerings of perfume and so forth, accompanied by their respective mantras. In this regard, these are the mudrās and mantras: first, extending the hand like the sun, one should employ the perfume mudrā. [2] *Oṃ hūṃ svāhā*. This is the perfume. Having formed the perfume mudrā, one should join it with the white *jñāna* [mudrā].

Oṃ śrīṃ svāhā. Flower. Having formed the flower-mudrā, one should contract [the fingers] at the conch-flower. Oṃ a svāhā. Incense. Having joined the vajra-fists, with the thumbs raised toward the sun. Oṃ kṣuṃ svāhā. Lamp. Having made the añjali-gesture of the sun and moon, extending them inwardly polished; at the base of the root of impurity and smoke, it is joined with knowledge and realization. Oṃ i svāhā. Food offering.

Then, at the conclusion of the worship, having performed the *kamalāvarta* gesture and placed the vajra-añjali at the heart, one should prostrate with the five-fold maṇḍala: *oṃ namas te hūṃ, namāmi hūṃ, namo nama hūṃ svāhā*. Having thus prostrated, while remaining in that same position, one should again perform the three prostrations: *oṃ pañcaḍākinipūjopasthānāyātmānaṃ niryātayāmi*; *oṃ ācāryapūjopasthānāyātmānaṃ niryātayāmi*; *oṃ sakalasattvaparitrānārtham ātmānaṃ niryātayāmi*. *Samayas tvaṃ samaya hoḥ 3*.

Then, having visualized for the purification of body, speech, and mind the syllable *i*, the syllable *a*, and the syllable *ha* respectively within the three white solar discs situated at the head, throat, and heart, one should generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), even while remaining in that state, having gone for refuge.
I go for refuge forever to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; indeed,
to all those of the three vehicles, the Ḍākinīs of the secrets of yoga and so forth,
the Heroes, the Heroines, the Goddesses, and the great-souled Bodhisattvas.
But especially, I go for refuge to the Teacher constantly.
May all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, headed by Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnāgrya, Lokeśa, and Amoghasiddhi, attend to me; I [am]... [for the sake of... through [my] devotion.
I generate the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening,
just as the Protectors of the three times resolved upon perfect enlightenment.
I firmly undertake the threefold morality, patience, and diligence, as well as the welfare of sentient beings and the activities for their benefit.
From this day forward, I shall undertake the vow born of the yoga of the Buddha, toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha— the supreme and unsurpassed Triple Gem.
Having accepted the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā,
I shall receive the Ācārya consecration in the exalted assembly of the Great Vajra Family.
I shall bestow the fourfold gift six times every day,
within the yoga of the Great Jewel Family and the delightful samaya.
I receive the true Dharma— outer, secret, and belonging to the three vehicles—
within the pure Mahāpadma family, which gives birth to great awakening.
I truly undertake the vow associated with all [the families],
performing the rite of worship according to my ability within the exalted assembly of the great family of rites.
Having generated the supreme, unsurpassed mind of enlightenment,
I have undertaken the complete vow for the sake of all sentient beings.
"I shall cause those who have not crossed over to cross; I shall liberate those who are not liberated;
I shall give comfort to those who are comfortless; and I shall establish sentient beings in nirvana."
Then,
having first extended the moon and sun, encircled by wisdom and discernment,
one should form the shape of a swan’s wing by turning it within the heart.
With this great armor mudrā and with this mantra:
*oṃ hūṃ he phaṭ*. [3]

Then, when the moon has been made by the sun and moon, one should whirl the smoke, which is free from the three impurities and joined with the sound of the syllable *hūṃ*, like a wheel in all directions.
Thus, by means of this seal (*mudrā*) pertaining to all protections,

one should briefly perform, through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), the binding of the directions, the driving-in of the stakes (*kīla*), the enclosure wall (*prākāra*), the cage (*pañjara*), the maṇḍala, and so forth.

Then, established in the mudrā of meditative concentration, with his gaze fixed upon his own cross-legged posture, he should rest upon the fire of the syllable *kṣuṃ* within the radiance of his own heart; perceiving that which remains as the seed-syllable, having the nature of the signless gnosis-body (*jñānadeha*), he should meditate on the single equality of all phenomena, thinking: "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature."

Then, in order to produce the *dharmasaṃbhoga-kāya* which has emerged from the *dharmakāya*, one should instantly arouse oneself by means of the four goddesses, Vajraḍākinī and the others, who rely upon mental images; having been roused by their melodious songs of wisdom (*prajñāgītika*) in a low, warbling tone (*kākalīnāda*), which generate conceptualizations following upon the supramundane state, one should contemplate the self as mind.
This is the song of wisdom.
Ja ja ja ja! O Vajrasattva, grant me the siddhi of descent!
Ha ha ha ha! O Lord of the syllable Hūṃ, I am the pledge, I am the one who goes!
Va va va va! O Vajrasphoṭa, you who wear the secret body!
+ + + + + ho suto + vajra alim eka svalīyana hūṃ ||
Having thus recited these verses four times and considering himself as one whose conceptual constructions have been aroused, he rose.

Then, having visualized a white lotus transformed from the syllable *hrīḥ*, which has the desired extent of the path of Rudra; and within that, a wind-maṇḍala by means of the syllable *yuṃ*; and within that, a circle of white light; and above that, a pale lord of serpents, from which the primordial vajra is transformed; and then, having for a moment focused on that which fills the hollows of the sky with a mass of vajra-rays emanating therefrom—

Filling its interior with that [light] being withdrawn, one should visualize the vajra; having resolved that its own radiance is one's own self, one should generate the mantra-ego-sense (*mantrāhaṃkāra*) by reciting:
*oṃ vajraśuddhāḥ sarvadharmā vajraśuddho ’ham*.

Furthermore, having ascertained oneself as the Great Vajradhara, who emerges from the vajra and is the perfection of the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) resulting from the maturation of the enjoyment of the Dharma, one should recite the mantra:
*oṃ yogaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmā yogaśuddho ’ham*.

Then, by means of the application of Vajragandhā, he beheld [the deity] resembling a jasmine flower or the moon, seated upon a lotus throne, with a body radiating the brilliance of a diamond, a face graced by an amorous smile, and established in the Lalitarāja posture.
Clad in silk garments, adorned with royal ornaments,
[he saw] the divine Hara, wearing a crown of the five Buddhas.

Thus, having clearly taken hold of the Mahāmudrā, one should seal it with the four mudrās. In this regard, the sequence is as follows: in one’s own heart, upon a moon disk consisting of the syllable *hūṃ* and the five [syllables], one should visualize the wisdom-finger that indicates knowledge and non-knowledge.

Having fashioned the earth as the parasol, the lotus as the needle, and the three impurities as the smoke-bannered fire, she stands at the destruction within the needle; having pierced [it], she is established in the heart.

*vajrasattva dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ samayas tvaṃ samayam ahaṃ a 3* | *oṃ vajrasattva aḥ svāhā* | Having thus practiced the heart mantra (*hṛdayamantra*) three times, and having accomplished the mantra through the recitation of the *dharmamudrā*, one should meditate on the end of the path.

Then, having visualized within one's own heart a universal trident-vajra transformed from the internal vowel, the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) is that which is endowed with its own insignia, possesses the five-pronged [vajra] as the gesture of the emblem (cihnamudrā), and so forth.

Then, preceded by the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), one should perform the empowerment of the three bodies (*trikāyādhiṣṭhāna*). In that regard, having performed the turning of the wheel at the site of the empowerment of the digits (*kalā*), one should unite the conch with gnosis (*jñāna*).
By means of this, one should place the eight seed-syllables of the Yoginīs upon the limbs.
Thus, with the *yākalanamudrā* bound,
one should place the syllable *kṣuṃ* on the head, the syllable *hūṃ* on the two eyes,
and the brilliantly blazing *suṃ* on the ears, the nose, the interior [of the body], and the tongue.
One should place *smryuṃ* on the neck, *ymryuṃ* on the chest,
*ymryuṃ* on the region of the heart, and *kṣmryuṃ* on the navel.
Thus, having sequentially performed the ritual assignment of the limbs for the purification of body, speech, and mind.
Oṃ vajrakāya hoḥ | Oṃ vajravākyāya aḥ | Oṃ vajrahṛdaye hūṃ |
One should consecrate [it] with this mantra.
Having formed two vajra-fists, one should raise the white *rocanā*; having kissed the tips of those two, one should raise the smoke and the three impurities.
When she is situated in the five places, her own peak is colored by the Sage.
Thus, with this initiation mudrā and the mantra *oṃ hūṃ aḥ svāhā*, one should perform the consecration.
Having formed two vajra-fists, with the white [thumb] and the yellow [forefinger] raised,
one should rotate the two [fists] and bind them at the crown of the head, on the back, and at the heart;
by means of this armor mudrā.
Oṃ ṭaṭṭaṃ hūṃ svāhā. Thus one should don the armor.
Then...
Oṃ hūṃ svāhā— having thus recited this while holding the silk ribbon.
Oṃ vajra tuṣya hor.
Thus, one should satisfy [the deity] with the abode of equanimity.
When the moon is equal to the sun and moon, [one should offer] a sign of the impurity of mere smoke.
With this mudrā, one should offer the overflowing water for the *argha* and fragrance.
*Oṃ pratīccha arghaṃ hūṃ svāhā*.
Having offered the *argha* with the mantra and having worshipped [the deity] as before with perfumes and other offerings;
Having formed this Vajramuṣṭi mudrā, one should apply it with pride at the waist, accompanied by the *lāsya* dance and the mantra: *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*.
Having extended the "moon-hand" (candrahasta) joined with the knowledge of the gesture of breaking,
and having grasped the fragrant conch (gandhaśaṅkha) with the "sun-hand" (sūryahasta), one should scatter it with the mantra:
*oṃ supriyagandhe hūṃ maḥ*, using the fragrance.
O Raṇḍā, having placed that which has come from the three impurities of consciousness into the hand of Candra,
one should strike with the Khaṭaka gesture raised in the hand of Sūrya,
using the mantra "Oṃ Hūṃ Ho Svāhā" and the lute.
Having formed a hollow with the two hands like the sun and moon, one should lift them upward and cast [the offering] with the mantra "Oṃ śrīṃ svāhā," using flowers.
The Gītāmudrā should be white; having moved it before the mouth with the mantra "Oṃ Hūṃ 3 Svāhā," [one should perform] the song.
Firmly grasping the vajra-fist with the moon,
one should seize it with the mantra "Oṃ iṃ svāhā" and with worship.
One should place the moon-hand on the right hip;
having placed the sun-hand, one should hold it upon his head.
With the mantra "HŪṂ SVĀHĀ," one should perform the dance through dancing.
Placing the *añjali* at the crown of the head is proclaimed as the lamp mudrā;
[this is performed] with the mantra "Oṃ kṣuṃ svāhā" by means of the lamp.
Thus, having performed the worship with the eightfold mantras and mudrās,
the wise one should then take up the vajra and bell according to the reality.
Having extended the solar portion, one should join it with the white command;
its smoke being raised, this is proclaimed as the Vajra-mudrā— by means of this [mudrā].
One should take up the vajra with this mantra: *oṃ hūṃ*.
In his application with the moon, the bell-seal (ghaṇṭāmudrā) is proclaimed;
by means of this [seal] and with this mantra, "Oṃ hoḥ svāhā," one should take up the bell.

Having formed two vajra-fists, one should conquer by placing them back-to-back. Raising a white *rocanā* [pigment], surrounded by a lotus and a hundred earths, one should cause it to move together with the sounds of "dhūṃ"; thus one is worshipped by all the Buddhas.
Thus, with the *baddhacālanamudrā*.
Oṃ vajraghaṇṭe hūṃ hoḥ | Oṃ vajraghaṇṭe raṇita praraṇita sarvabuddhapracālite prajñāpāramitānādasvabhāve vajradharahṛdayāvasantoṣaṇi hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ svāhā—thus one should ring the bell.
With the movement of trembling and pervading, the secret pair of lotuses is seized;
Vajrasattva shines as the supreme state beyond the supreme.
Thus, one should consecrate with this Mahāmudrā.
Then, having formed the very same Ghaṇṭāmudrā as previously described, one should sound that very bell.
O hero, abandon the sight of the eyes of those capable [of passion];
let the syllable of the nature of reality be heard in the play of emptiness.
One should discern the middle way, which is liberated from both existence and non-existence;
having reflected upon it, one should break through every single syllable.
In the harsh waters of worldly existence,
dharma is like a mother who, though unloved and unknown, brings about the fruit of liberation.
O Yoginī, you who are intoxicated by the nature of all things, you dance like one deluded by the pleasures of saṃsāra and striving for liberation.
The fivefold yoga is perceived as the reality of the Buddha; it is attained by the Mother through beings of many various forms.
O virtuous lady, you who have accomplished your duty through the discernment of Dharma;
I bow to you, the yoginī who has crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra and attained liberation.
Homage be to you, Lord of Yoga, liberator of beings!
Homage be to you, the Son of All, through your singular nature!
Homage be to you, the cutter of the delusion of saṃsāra!
Homage be to the One Reality; I always bow down to it.
Thus, at the conclusion of the offering of hymns, having performed the Mahāmudrā, one who abides on the level of the Peak of Existence [strives] for the purification of all Buddha-fields.
Reciting the mantra "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature," one should repeatedly bring the equality of all phenomena to mind.
By this much, the preliminary yoga becomes fully cultivated. || o ||
Furthermore, remaining thus in the expanse of space, [he acts] for the sake of the gradual purification of the three realms of existence.
Yūṃ: the wind mandala is bow-shaped and red.
KṢŪM: a yellow triangular fire-mandala.
The water mandala is circular and white.
Hūṃ! The great mandala of the earth, shining like the essence of the moon and a bee.
Above that, with the syllable *suṃ* alone, one should visualize the great ocean filled with milk;
in its center, with the syllable *hūṃ*, one should visualize the great Mount Meru made of the seven precious gems.
Having done so, one should form the hand palm-upward and imagine it as a vajra. [6]
Having expanded [the consciousness] through the five locations, one performs the purification of the seven netherworlds.
Having thus empowered [the ground] with this mudrā for purifying the site, which is placed upon the summit of Mount Meru, reciting: *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*.
With that, [he touches] the head of the *mālatī*.
A city made of the essence of wind, fashioned at will,
its quarters occupied by ḍākinīs, and variegated with the splendor of the seven jewels.
It is square, with four gates, adorned with four archways,
graced by dangling necklaces and half-necklaces, and made resonant by a network of tinkling bells.
The water-pot (kumbha) is resplendent with eight lotuses (*ambuja*) that have emerged, their tops marked by a lion, a peacock, a bull, a swan, and a fish.
Having thus observed the outer city— with its turrets, junctions, corners, and peaks, and with the crescent moon, vajra, and pestle— [one should then observe] the inner city once more.
Having first contemplated a square on all four sides divided into five parts,
one should exclude the middle section and have it encircled by two [lines] within that space.
Visualizing the outer circular mandala of the yoginīs,
and within that, a nine-square grid adorned with vajras.
It is square, with four gates, and devoid of archways;
it is adorned with crossed vajras (viśvavajra) placed at its four corners.
One should construct the excellent door with a fifth part of the circle;
the chest (urasa) is joined with half of that, and the pedestal (vedikā) is half the size of the chest.
One should arrange the dust-floor everywhere using half of the altar;
the first circle is the color of the directions, and the second is crimson-red.
The third [city] is dark blue like the sky, and its fillet is golden and reddish;
one should always conceive of the city of the Great Yogīśvarīs in this manner.
Thus, having visualized the peaked pavilion.
In the central chamber, a lion throne; in the eastern chamber, an elephant throne;
in the northern chamber, a peacock throne.
In the western petal, Ga...
[8] Pratyālīḍha posture: restrained by the ālīḍha stance. Standing restrained by the pratyālīḍha stance, one shall strike down the obstructors in the center and below with the mantra: *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*.
Having formed two vajra-fists, one should raise the Knowledge and Wisdom [fingers];
then, like a parasol upon the earth, one should encircle the lotus-needle in all directions like a wheel.
Thus, having formed the great enclosure seal (*mahāprākāramudrā*) and established the enclosure with the mantra *oṃ jambhani hūṃ phaṭ*, [one should proceed].

Having made the "Sūryahasta" (Sun-hand) gesture with the palm facing upward, one should strike the ground; by performing this, it is the *kīlanamudrā* (nailing mudrā). Having nailed [the site] with the mantra *oṃ hraṃ phaṭ*, one should extend the "Sūryacandra" (Sun-moon) gesture upward and touch the tip with the front [of the hand]; by means of this, it is the *pañjaramudrā* (cage mudrā).
Oṃ jruṃ svāhā. Thus, one should bestow the cage.

Then, as before, having armored oneself with the Great Armor (mahākavaca) and commencing the Great Yoga, one is conjoined with the Sattva-mudrā; surrounded as before by the four Ḍākinīs suspended [in space], one should bring external emptiness (bahirdhā-śūnyatā) to manifestation.
One should recite the mantra: "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature."

Then, one should swiftly cause oneself, the body of beings, and the fourth ḍākinī to move; having visualized the syllable ĀLI in the sky of one’s own heart, its center occupied by the syllable HŪṂ, through the yoga of the wheel.
As before, having generated [the deity] with "ja ja je," and so forth, one should visualize the body of gnosis (*jñānadeha*) as having the nature of a mirror, appearing as a white lunar disc.
One should say: "Jñāno haṃ āḥ.

Furthermore, having placed Kālikā above that through the yoga of the maṇḍala, and having superposed it upon the center of the heart, one should generate a five-pronged vajra marked by a lunar disc produced from its transformation; having superposed the heart upon the center of that [vajra], one should resolve upon the state of the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*).
One should recite the mantra: "Oṃ, all phenomena are vajra-pure; I am vajra-pure."
Then one should utter "Vajra Haṃ Āḥ.

Then, having radiated forth rays of light in the form of vajras, and having withdrawn back into those very [rays] the Tathāgatas and the activities—such as the maturing of various world-systems—that had been accomplished through their mouths, one should visualize a vajra composed of the atoms of all the Tathāgatas. Focusing on the nourishment of its nature as the [wisdom of] discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā*), one should recite: "Oṃ vartamāno haṃ hor."
Then, that [mind] having been perfected through the performance of duties, it becomes a sword.
He has three faces and six arms, with a luster like that of a dense, dark cloud;
he possesses three eyes, is smiling yet wrathful, and is colored by the sentiment of erotic passion (*śṛṅgārarasa*).
Seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, with a skull as his prominent crown-ornament,
his body radiates the rays of the Victors, and he is closely embraced by the limb of Wisdom.
One should meditate upon the Lord, whose body is the essence of the yoga of sages, bearing a vajra at the position of the breasts, a bell, a vessel, and a bow.
Thus, having taken recourse to the self as the sky of yoga,
one should perform the ego-identification with: *oṃ udbhavo haṃ a ā ū ūṃ hūṃ svāhā*.
Then, one should cause [the practitioner] to enter into the state of the utterly pure realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Uttering the mantra "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga," while brandishing the vajra, one should again form the ego-identification: "Oṃ, I am the Gnosis Body."
Then,
having joined it with the lotus-knowledge and joined it with the parasol-knowledge,
one should fasten a chain with the two [remaining] [knowledges], and make the rest into banners.
Holding the smoke-indicating needle of the three impurities and the five-pronged vajra;
thus it is recited. [End of 8]
[6] The pentad of the Buddha-cloud-floods.
Having withdrawn [the elements] by means of the yoga of the mass, one should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord, the sky of the yoga of the Buddha,
through the state of being that is existence, according to the description of the previous characteristics.
One should meditate with unwavering and undisturbed contemplation upon the body whose nature is wisdom and means, which is intent on the radiance of the ḍākinīs and others.
In the four directions and in the auspicious locations, [one should establish] the unborn [deities] with their respective mantras,
possessing the nature of firmness through the yoga of radiating and reabsorbing.
One should place Vajrī, Ghorī, Vetālī, and Caṇḍālī on the right side;
they are white, yellow, red, and blue in color, and are most terrifying.
Having expanded the Lalita, Ardhaparyaṅka, Utkaṭa, and Jānūāsana postures, and having [visualized] the one with disheveled hair who wears the crest-ribbon of the Lord of her own family;
The white smoke, as well as the conch and lotus, have the nature of the channels;
on the right are the lotus-vessels, and on the left is the holder of the khaṭvāṅga.
Having generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), which accomplishes the vision of primordial wisdom,
and having joined it to the eightfold path, which accomplishes the awakening of a Buddha.
One should assign the deities to the intermediate directions with mantras consisting of four-syllable kūṭas:
Siṃhī, Vyāghrī, Śivā, and Lūkī, well-established in their respective places.
Their colors are white and yellow, black and white, and red and black, respectively.
One should contemplate this color as being red, yellow, and variegated.
A lion, a buffalo, a boar, and Śiva seated upon his throne;
