But the fifth is "always luminous," resembling the cloudless firmament.

Having raised it, one should place it in various locations. When the yogin places it in the eyes, divine vision (*divyacakṣus*) arises; in the ears, divine hearing (*divyaśrotra*) that reaches all sounds; in the nostrils, divine smell (*divyaghrāṇa*); in the tongue, excellence in perceiving tastes and divine speech (*divyavāṇī*); in the skin, a divine body (*divyakāya*); and likewise, when placed on the head, there is knowledge of the transition of the body, the intermediate states, the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and the three times.

In the throat, one should mention poetic skill and knowledge of one's own and others' tenets; in the heart, sentient beings, the superknowledges, the increase of sacrifice, and mindfulness; in the navel, the inexhaustibility of acting for the benefit of all sentient beings and omniscience.

Thus, with a mind stabilized and having obtained all the jewels of qualities, one attains Buddhahood. Even when arisen from yoga, one should resolve that all phenomena consist of great bliss and have the nature of the Dharmakāya. Again, the practice of meditative absorption and again the practice of arising from it should be performed according to one's ability with a concentrated mind. In this way, through these two yogas, like the continuous flow of a river or the succession of lamp-flames, remaining constantly in yoga, one stands before the Great One.
Thus, through such practice, even for a yogin of little merit, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā arises in no time at all. And it has been said:
See, hear, endure, eat;
smell, wander, sit, and stand.
Speak using only the conventional expressions *āla* and *māla*; do not let the mind-chamber (*manachattra*) waver from its single-pointed state.
It is to be understood from the instruction of the guru. Thus ends the fourth [chapter], the Jñānakauñcikā. O.

Oṃ, ma—thus: a, u, m. A is Akṣobhya, u is Vairocana, and m is Ratnapadmarāja. The conjunction of these is the syllable Oṃ. It represents the body, speech, and mind; the three worlds; the three principles (tattvas); the three times; and the triple realm. It is the worship and sovereignty of all that exists.

Regarding the term "tree": it is the single tree consisting of the leaves, fruits, flowers, and [essence] of the non-dual mind-tree. The letter *e* is loving-kindness (*maitrī*); the letter *ka* is compassion (*karuṇā*); the letter *vṛ* is sympathetic joy (*muditā*); the letter *kṣa* is equanimity (*upekṣā*). With minds directed toward these, the mantra-practitioner should rely upon the tree of the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*).

Thereafter, having relied upon the tree of the accumulation of gnosis (*jñāna-sambhāra*), one should unify the four drops—the drop of application (*prayoga-bindu*) by means of the letter *e*, the root-drop (*maula-bindu*) by means of the letter *ka*, the subsequent drop (*pṛṣṭha-bindu*) by means of the letter *vṛ*, and the drop for the benefit of beings (*sattvārtha-bindu*) by means of the letter *kṣa*—and thus the two trees, which are the expansion of the three times. And it is said:
The tree of the non-dual mind stands supreme, spreading throughout the three worlds; it bears the blossoms and fruits of compassion and is adorned with the excellence of self-restraint.

It is further stated: *E* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); *Ka* is signlessness (*ānimitta*); *Vṛ* is wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); *Kṣa* is lack of volitional construction (*anabhisaṃskāra*). The tree of supreme emptiness, with its flowers of compassion, is bent down by the fruit of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*). The yogin who possesses the power of that tree attains the siddhi of Mahāmudrā. Thus it has been said.
The tree of emptiness has blossomed with the various wonders of compassion;
its flowers are the expansion of the command and the state of other-power—this is the mind consisting of supreme bliss.

Furthermore, *saṃ* has the nature of the Saṃbhogakāya, which is like a vessel for the bodhicitta of pure awareness (*saṃvitti*). *Karu* has the nature of the Dharmakāya, which is endowed with bliss and compassion (*karuṇā*). Because it proceeds from that dual mind, or because of compassion for the sake of sentient beings, there is the syllable *vṛ*. *Kṣa* is the form of great emptiness (*mahāśūnya*), in which all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) reach dissolution and enter into absorption (*laya*).

Then, because that great emptiness is devoid of form, flowers, fruits, leaves, branches, and roots, the practitioner of mantra does not become liberated from both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa by means of that object of focus. Thus it has been said:
In that empty forest of trees where compassion has blossomed from its root,
where the *ālā* creeper weaves its own bower, one who falls there is struck by calamity.

*E* is wisdom (*prajñā*), *ka* is skillful means (*upāya*), *vṛ* is the moon (*candra*), and *kṣa* is the sun (*sūrya*). By that, from the seed of the power of cultivation, the threefold tree is born; it bears fruit in the form of the fruit of non-abiding, whose nature is emptiness and compassion. Thus it has been said:
The seed is one, the cause is another, and the fruit is one;
he who hears this as it is distinguished is liberated from the cycle of existence.
It is to be understood through the instruction of a guru regarding each individual yoga. || o ||

Regarding the word *śmaśāna*: the letter *sa* is the essence of the body (*kāyatattva*), the letter *ma* is the essence of speech (*vāktattva*), and the letter *na* is the essence of mind (*cittatattva*); thus, these three syllables are the protectors of the cremation ground.
O Lord, playing in the cremation ground (śmaśāna) together with the Jñāna-ḍākinīs;
because one breathes there, it is designated as the "cremation ground" (śmaśāna).
With a mind focused on the aesthetic stage, the practitioner of mantra [should contemplate] that which pervades all the limbs and minor parts of the body.
With his face turned toward it, while the world of the three times is being dissolved without remainder,
one should worship the Lord situated therein, accompanied by the moon and flowers.
By that merit, he shall become [the Buddha] and attain the hand-mudrās.
Thus it has been said:
Abandon body, speech, and mind; remain silent and dwell in non-falsehood.
One should perform such actions as are appropriate; for one who is resolute, [the goal] will be attained after a long time.
Thus ends the yoga of the cremation ground. o ||
Regarding "Parvata": in the root *parv*, which contains the letter *pa* representing space (*viyat*), the letter *rvva* is designated as the person (*puruṣa*).
That bliss is identical with it; the letter *ta* indicates that [bliss] throughout the three times.
...the mountain known as Pāpaprakṣālana-parvata,
which is like a peak of Mount Trikūṭa and is truly a vast treasury of happiness.
In this regard, this is the unsurpassed state for one who dwells on the mountain and has cast off [all] bonds.
The barley-recitation was for great happiness; the sky was beautiful.
On that day, Rāvaṇa was abandoned along with his natural beauty by the Yoginī.
Thus ends the yoga of Parvata.
Regarding "kandara":
they say the letter *ka* is the bodhicitta, while the letter *da* is the avadhūtī;
the letter *ra* is the sahaja-caṇḍālī, who, having nourished [them], resides in the three wheels.

"Joined with the beauty of many mountain regions, flowing with the water of nectar, and equal to the moving moon"—thus, at the instruction regarding the cave, it should be contemplated for a long time by the yogin with a concentrated mind. So it has been said:
This very moon, the lord of the night, having drunk the water of the mountain streams of the sky, now desires to rest upon the mountain peaks.

Thus ends the *kandara-yoga*. Regarding the term *guhya*: the syllable *gu* is the wisdom (*prajñā*) of the moon-maṇḍala, which has the nature of the synthesis of all Buddhas. The syllable *hūṃ* is the means (*upāya*) of the sun-maṇḍala, which has the nature of the singular synthesis of all Tathāgatas. Between them, one should visualize the two seed-syllables, which are the harshness of the bliss of the Dharma, adorned with lunar drops (*bindu*). Within the union of those two, through penetration, embracing, and investigation, the secret abode (*guhyāvāsa*) is revealed beyond that. As it has been said:
The fierce sun, having ground it with its rays, crushes it;
it sells both sin and merit as a commodity.

[12] Wealth and so forth are the limbs; emptiness and so forth are the liberations. Having thus visualized the empty house, which is the nature of the fourfold gnosis of the Buddha, one should emanate from the rays of light issuing from the seed-syllable all the Tathāgatas together with the Bodhisattvas, appearing in the form of a garland of heroes and yoginīs. Having gathered back those who have accomplished the welfare of the world—those who hold the nectar of the gnosis of all the Victors—one should meditate upon the four wheels as long as desired.
One should cultivate this with devotion, continuously, and for a long time; then the attainment of the four bodies will be accomplished in this very life. Thus it has been said:
The Lord of the Day (the Sun) has set; the boatman has abandoned the ferry.
He stands in his state of non-creation, yet by him the circle of the mandala was fashioned. o ||

Thus concludes the yoga of the dwelling devoid of distinctions. Regarding the term "vessel" (*bhājana*): the syllable *bhā* is the light of the *kakkola*; the syllable *ja* is the fire of the *vajra*; and the syllable *na* resides upon the head of the jewel-lotus in the form of the innate (*sahaja*). Then, one should meditate on the play of the *kakkola* and the *bola*, or rather, the play of wisdom and means as the *bola* descends from the navel to the heart. Through the power of such meditation, one should bring the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) face to face.

Having somehow brought [the mind] face-to-face, one should expand it through all the major and minor limbs and throughout all phenomena in the ten directions. One should perceive the great bliss that is mere luminosity devoid of objective referents for as long as one is able. Furthermore, wherever the channels, sense faculties, and objects are indeed consumed by fire, right there they should be understood as the vessel; the external is equal to that. Thus it has been said:
Salute that wish-fulfilling gem which bestows the fruit of one's desires, wherein the bliss of existence and nirvāṇa shine forth as one within the mind.
The mind is bound by bondage and liberated by liberation; of this there is no doubt. By that very thing through which the ignorant are bound, the awakened are swiftly set free. || 10 ||

Thus ends the section on the Vessel Yoga. Regarding the phrase "the stage situated on *tha*": by the syllable *tha*, there is the purity of the eye and eye-consciousness, which is Mohavajra (Vajra of Delusion). By the syllable *la*, there is the purity of the ear and ear-consciousness, which is Dveṣavajra (Vajra of Hatred). By the syllable *ga*, there is the purity of the nose and nose-consciousness, which is Mātsaryavajra (Vajra of Avarice). By the syllable *ta*, there is the purity of the mouth and tongue-consciousness, which is Rāgavajra (Vajra of Passion). By the syllable *bhū*, there is the purity of all limbs and body-consciousness, which is Īrṣyāvajra (Vajra of Envy).

By means of the syllable *ma*, one should expand the purification of the mind and mental consciousness as Śrī Heruka through the non-dual yoga of wisdom and method; thus, one should effect the three worlds as being composed of that [Heruka] by pervading the ten directions, which is the lineage of the Mothers (*mātasantati*). Through this, one attains the non-abiding nirvāṇa. Thus it is said: "Established upon the surface. This has been stated.
Whatever limb or whatever part may perish day by day, that very thing is satisfied;
O Lord of the Ascetics, no one asks about it. o ||

Thus ends the yoga of the stage of what has reached the surface (thalagatabhūmiyoga). Regarding "Mātaṅga": *mātaṃ* is the red essence of the sun; *gataṃ* is the white essence of the moon. The seed-syllable situated in their midst is deposited within the *mātaṅgas*. Having seen that supreme reality, which possesses the form of the innate (*sahaja*) at the pinnacle of the phonemes—shining, free from discursive elaboration, radiant—one emits the drop (*bindu*).
Having observed that line of light rising up—not too long—resembling a fine rod of Mahendra-blue sapphire, one perceives that its upward extension has the nature of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*).

One should meditate upon the nature of the *bhiṇḍima*—the form of self-reflexive awareness whose intrinsic nature is the limbs [of the deity], the very essence of the *dharmakāya*, consisting of great bliss, having the heart-essence of the Great Vajradhara, and possessing the nature of Śrī Heruka; this self, having expanded its continuum, pervades the entire world as the supreme secret form. Therein, one should visualize the *bhara* (the seed-syllable) as a *yantrikā* (a mechanical device) like a bee, revolving within the shape of a "well-being" (*svastika*) of bliss situated in the sheath of the *ūrṇā* (the hair-treasure between the eyebrows), moving upward.

The practitioner, with a concentrated mind, should gaze for as long as he is able until the mind becomes stable. Once the mind has become stable, he should recognize it by means of signs, as described previously. Thus it has been said:
Just as it is outside, so it is within;
throughout the fourteen worlds, it is entirely without interval.
Someone without a body is hidden within the body;
he who knows that is liberated therein.

With these twelve places, one should instantly resolve that oneself is Jñāneśvarī. In a tree, a cremation ground, a mountain, a cave, a secret place, the outskirts of a village, on a path, a field, an empty house, [or] a vessel, on ground situated on dry land—one should consecrate [the site] with the specific Mātaṅga mantras. Thus ends the Mātaṅga yoga.

In the center is Jñānaḍākinī, black, with three faces and six arms, holding a banner (*ketu*), noose, sword, axe, vajra, and bell. In the east is Śuklavajraḍākinī, white, with one face and a banner in her hand. In the north is Ghorāḍākinī, yellow, with one face, a banner, and a yogic vessel (*yogapātra*) in her hands. In the west is Vettālaḍākinī, red, with a banner and a skull-cup (*karoṭa*) in her hands. In the south is Caṇḍālāḍākinī, black, with a banner and a skull-cup in her hands. In the northeast is Siṃhinī, white and yellow, with a banner and a needle (*sūcī*).

In the southeast is Vyāghrī, white and black, holding a banner and a noose in her hands. In the southwest is Jambukī, blue and red, holding a banner and a sword in her hands. In the northwest is Ulūkinī, red and yellow, holding a *khaṭvāṅga* and a vajra in her hands. Their seats, in order, are a lion, an elephant, a peacock, a garuḍa, and a servant; furthermore, there are the seats of a lion, a vajra-beaked bird, a buffalo, and a jackal.

In the eastern chamber is Kṛṣṇarudra, who is blue and surrounded by Śvetacāmuṇḍā and others, holding flowers, incense, lamps, and perfumes in their hands. In the north is Mahārudra, who is yellow; [he is accompanied by] Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā, who are yellow, each with her own color and her hands occupied with her respective attributes. In the west is Devadatta, who is white; Bhadrakālī, Mahākālī, Sthūlakālī, and Yoginī are red. In the south is the one named Kṛṣṇa, who is red; Indrī, Candrī, Ghorī, Lambakī, and Kṛṣṇā are black.

In the northeast, Karāla is black and yellow; Kambojī, Dīpi, and Cūṣiṇī are the color of jasmine and the moon. In the southeast, Bhībhatsa is black and red; Ghorarūpā, Mahārūpā, Daṃṣṭrarūpā, Karālanī, and Nīlā are blue. In the southwest, Nandātīta is red and white; Kapālamālā, Mālinī, Khaṭvāṅgā, and Yamaharddhikā are red in color.

In the northwest is Vināyaka, white and yellow; [the others] have a khaṭvāṅga in hand, an axe in hand, a vajra in hand, and a bow in hand, and are golden-colored. All of these have their hands occupied with the five offerings. Through the purification of the eight [syllables], there are the eight Bhairavas. Arisen from the first syllable of each name, they have one face and four arms, and possess a trident as their banner.
The mantra-practitioner desiring accomplishment should show [the mandala] to those belonging to the mandala.
One should offer the eightfold worship beginning with *lāsya*, preceded by the *kamalāvarta* dance,
to the deities of the maṇḍala with one's whole being according to reality.
Then, one should worship all the deities with twenty offerings.
Then there were lutes, flutes, sacrificial ladles, small drums, fans, banners, kettledrums, bronze gongs, parasols, canopies, and small flags.

She is graceful through dance, laughter, and amorous charm; she is terrifying through anger, wrath, and fear; yet she is compassionate toward the mental continuums of all sentient beings, bestowing the gift of the Dharma.
They have pacified the primary and secondary afflictions and are established in the reality of peace.
Then, with an offering of praise accompanied by the sounding of the vajra and bell,
one should laud the deities of the maṇḍala for the sake of achieving the success of one's ritual activities.
One should grasp the vajra with its true essence, ring the bell according to the Dharma,
and form the Mahāmudrā through the commitment (samaya) by means of the visualization of one's respective mantras.
The being without beginning or end, Vajrasattva, the great hero,
Samantabhadra, the soul of all, the lord of the pride of the vajra— this is Vajrasattva, my [self].
Beings have the characteristic of space, and space is also without characteristics;
through union with the equality of space, the equality of all that is supreme is made manifest.

Oṃ vajraghaṇṭe raṇita prataṇita saṃpraṇita, you who stir the minds of all Tathāgatas, you who cause Vajrasattva to enter the heart, by the intrinsic nature of the sound of Prajñāpāramitā: Āḥ Hūṃ 3 Hoḥ Ṭakki Jaḥ Hoḥ. Thus is the reality of the bell.
Having brandished the vajra according to its true nature through the yoga of uplifting it to the heart,
one should hold it with the application of pride in the bell, through meditations on reality.
In the city accompanied by Māmakī, one should cause [the disciple] to recite the pride of Vajrasattva and the vajra-bell with the meditations on the reality of consciousness. O ||
The three syllables SU-KHA-TRĪ represent the glorious forms of body, speech, and mind;
they are the erotic, the wrathful, and the laughing, possessing three eyes and bodies as magnificent as the luster of sapphire.
The six excellent arms, marked with the six signs, hold the six earths.
He holds a skull-topped staff, a begging bowl, a sword, a flaying knife, and a vajra-bell;
he is the one who cuts through the turmoil of hell with his cries of "Hā!
Hā!", and he is the supreme savior who bestows liberation upon the world.
O Jñāna-Ḍākinī, to you whose pair of feet is worthy of salutation, I pay homage.
The glorious embodiment of the body, possessing the color that pacifies all evils;
bearing the khaṭvāṅga, the supreme vessel of wine, and the skull-cup;
the remover of the afflictions of the great ocean of the sea of saṃsāra.
O Vajraḍākinī, whose pair of feet is worshipped!

He who possesses the excellent form of the glorious Dharmamūrti and bears a beautiful countenance; who holds aloft the khaṭvāṅga staff and carries a skull-bowl filled with the essence of the fierce sentiment;
and who effects the severing of the bonds of existence for all the worlds.
O you whose pair of feet is saluted by Vetālas and Ḍākinīs!
The illustrious Karmamūrti, whose speech is like that of Hari, possessing an unfailing form;
bearing a khaṭvāṅga, a fierce nose, and a skull;
he who severs the bonds of existence arising from afflictions such as passion.
O Caṇḍālī-Dākinī, whose pair of feet is saluted!
To Śrī, Siṃhī, Vyāghrī, Varāhī, Jambukī, and Lūkinī;
to those who destroy all wicked beings with the threatening gesture and the noose;
and to those who hold the sword and the goad in their right hands.
O you who possess forearms like the handles of axes that sever the wicked,
O you who destroy all the manifold sufferings of separation,
O illusory-formed one whose pair of feet is worshipped— I bow to you!
O you who are honored by the *ḍākinīs*, O you who shine brightly, O you who drink [the nectar],
O you who belong to Kamboja, O protectress of the world, O fierce one with a crown,
O destroyer of the strength of others who are difficult to tame and wicked!
Having bowed down to everything at the pair of feet of the goddess and the ḍākinīs.
With garments and ornaments made of mind, with the sounds of songs of beautiful words and the dancing of young women,
and with various excellent flowers and pungent incense;
The lamp of the supreme knowledge of light, possessing a fragrant scent.
The wheel of the application of the supreme yoginīs, the secret of the Lord of Energy;
the yoga, subsequent yoga, ultra-yoga, and great-super-yoga;
the discourse on the view of a real body, which is without devotion and eternally obscure.
I bow to the venerable Śrī Guhyapīṭha, who has performed the supreme worship.

The reality of the yoga of the movement and resonance of the venerable vajra-bell, belonging to the one whose body is radiant with the splendor of the most excellent seat of Śrī+hyā, the playful crown of the supreme lord Śrītattvarāja.
Thus [ends the section on] Śrījñānalābha Parameśvara, the enjoyer of worldly experience. o ||
In this way, one should satisfy the deities with the sounding of bells and hymns of praise;
then, one should perform worship again with the offerings of perfumes and other ritual services.
For the purpose of destroying the bondage of destiny, one should contemplate all phenomena as follows:
*oṃ suśuddhadharmatāsvabhāvo ’haṃ hūṃ, a ā ū ūṃ*.
In that very same way, one should indeed meditate upon all [deities] even within the fourfold yoga;
thereafter, having performed the rite of offering (bali), one should satisfy all those who bestow all things.
One should indeed recollect the fields (kṣetra), secondary fields (upakṣetra), meeting places (chandoha), and seats (pīṭha);
having invoked the deities there, accompanied by mantras and mudrās.
One should join the two fists of the sun and moon back-to-back;
encircling the lotus of the earth-parasol, the white one is raised upward.
Moving the white, curled [finger], it is supreme for attracting deities;
touching the vessel with the sun [the thumb] and raising the threatening finger toward the moon [the index finger]. O ||
Oṃ! At a solitary tree, or in a cremation ground, on a mountain, in a cave, or in a secret place;
by the side of a village, on a path, in a field, and especially in an empty house.
When the vessel has fallen upon the ground, especially if it is a vessel belonging to a Mātaṅga,
it is possessed by Kṛṣṇarudra, Mahārudra, and Devadatta.
Kṛṣṇa is the leader who is formidable, terrifying, and beyond all joy;
Cāmuṇḍī, Gaurī, and the goddess Umā likewise abide in a state of dreadfulness.
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā,
Bhadrakālī, Mahākālī, and Sthūlakālī are indeed the Yoginīs.
Indrī, Candrī, Ghorī, Duṣṭī, Lambakī, Tṛdaśeśvarī,
Kambojī, Dīpi, and Cūṣiṇyā— the Yoginīs residing in the villages;
those of terrible form, great form, fanged form, and the Skull-Bearer (Kapālinī).
Wearing garlands of skulls and garlands, they possess the great supernatural power of the khaṭvāṅga staff.
To the one with sword and axe in hand, likewise with vajra in hand and bow;
O great reality of the five ḍākinīs, you who accomplish all desired aims!
The Great Queen of the Yoga Maṇḍala is Vajreśvarī, the Sovereign;
likewise, she is the Tathāgata of the Great Body, the Stainless One who creates through yoga.
O Vajreśvarī, by this command, having summoned all the [deities] who pervade everything:
Oṃ kakkakaddhaṇa, babbabandhana, khakkhakhādana, of all my evil-doers, slay them! slay them! strike them down! accomplish this task of mine! hūṃ 3 phaṭ 3 svāhā!
By means of the seal of Ṭakkirāja, there is the pleasing of all deities;
then, having again held the bell, [one recites] "Paramādya" and so forth in detail.
O primordial supreme reality, O great passion, O great delight!
O Samantabhadra, the soul of all, O Lord of the Lord of Vajragarva!
O Supreme Being of Mind, foremost in meditative concentration, Vajra of vajras, of great power! Foremost in the conduct of Samantabhadra, you who utterly crush Māra!
O Great Awakening of all wrathful ones, Buddha born from the foremost of Buddhas,
Vajra-hūṃkāra, hūṃkāra, Lord of the World, Holder of the Jewel!

O Great Passion, O Great Bliss, Desire and Liberation, the Great Wealth! [13, ha metáloṃ... Forming the vajra-añjali mudrā: *oṃ suśuddhadharme hūṃ a ā ū ūṃḥ svāhā*. By this much, the Mahāyoga is completed and has been cultivated. *o*
Thus, from the point at which yoga has been cultivated, the "excessive yoga" (*atiyoga*), consisting of the worship of the four *bali* offerings, should also be meditated upon.

In this regard, the procedure is as follows: Having put on a fine turban and upper garment from the great stage, his body adorned with ornaments such as a crown and armlets, wearing a garland, his face fragrant, his body anointed with sandalwood paste, and bearing the pride (*ahaṃkāra*) of a practitioner (*yogin*), he should have the high umbrella raised by an assistant who bears the pride of Śakra and acts as a replica of himself; while being well-fanned by two [attendants] holding moving fly-whisks, who bear the pride of Brahmā born from the lotus; and [attended] by one who maintains the pride of Rudra.

Proclaiming his name with the words "Haraśira, he is indeed [Vajra]," and standing in the posture of the *lalitākṣepa* while brandishing a vajra and ringing a bell, he should place before him— facing east— a bowl filled to the brim with appropriate food such as rice cooked with milk (*ṣaṣṭhika*), accompanied by honey, molasses, ghee, milk, and rice-gruel (*peyā*), on a square maṇḍala made fragrant with white scents like sandalwood and strewn with a profusion of white flowers as an offering of the five services (*pañcopacāra*).
Having formed two vajra-fists, one should join them back-to-back.
This is the Earth-Canopy (bhūcchatrā) and Lotus-Encircler (padmaveṣṭā); it is raised up with white ointment (śvetārocanam).
With the hands white and slightly bent, this is the supreme mudrā for summoning the deity.
With this *vāhana-mudrā*,
one should invoke [the deity] with the mantra: *oṃ vattali mahāvattali hūṃ 3 jaḥ svāhā*.
Then Candra, having reproached Bhājana, raised Sūryavajramuṣṭiśvetā.

Oṃ vāhani mahāvāhani pretavāhani sūryacandrasiddhimukhi jayarājisomarāji umādevi gaṅga surāpitāgasaṃgha grahagaṇa sarvagaṇa patikārttika śrīśaśidevi agalo pagalo asurasurarājaḥ pukkasi mahāpukkasiḥ hūṃ ho ho ākarṣaṇi ākarṣaṇi samādhiye, hūṃ 3 jaḥ phaṭ svāhā.
Thus one should recite.
Then, [the mantra] previously bound, encircled with white *arocana*: "This supreme seal, called the *samaya*, is that which seizes the foremost deity.
Thus it was said.
Oṃ, consume, consume! O Lord of the Samaya, jruṃ phraṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Having thus recited the mantra and snapped the fingers three times, one should dismiss [the deities]. This concludes the offering to the deities.

Again, the yogin, standing with feet even and facing north, having performed the ritual in that same manner within the mandala and arranged offerings such as milk, he fills a vessel made of gold or similar material with [the substance] mixed with the three sweets. Having invoked [the deity] in the same way using the previously mentioned invocation mudrā and mantra, he forms the moon-fist (*candramuṣṭi*) and, having raised the sun-hand (*sūryapāṇi*) so that it is jagged with the consciousness of the parasol, joins it in the shape of a hood; this is the snake-mudrā (*phaṇimudrā*).

Oṃ! Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, Kuliśapāla, Devatī, Mahādevatī, Somaśikhi, Daṇḍadhara, Apalāla, Huluhulu, [Khaṇḍa], Sāgara, Mahāsāgara, Tapta, Mahātapta, Śrīkānti, Mahākānti, Ratnakānti, Surūpa, Mahāsurūpa, Bhadrāhika, Mahodara, Jhilli, Mahājhilli—Oṃ! Come, come, O lords of the great nāgas! All of you: Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Phraṃ Phuḥ Svāhā!
Having repeated this as before, one should dismiss [the deities]. Thus ends the Nāgabali.

Again, standing facing west, by means of throwing the mandala [of ashes], one should place before oneself—upon a triangular mandala made of red sandalwood and the like, strewn with red and yellow saffron—as previously described, boiled rice mixed with curd, honey, ghee, and the five nectars; then, remaining in that same position, one should invoke [the deity] with the aforementioned gesture of wrath and those very same mantra and mudrā.

Oṃ Māṇibhadra, Pūrṇabhadra, Subhadra, Jayabhadra, Nanda, Kīla, Mahākīla, Padmaśikha, Śaṅkhaśikha, Naṭa, Mahānaṭa, Bhedani, Chedani, Pūraṇi, Dhanādhanasudhana, Surūpa, Keli, Mahākeli, Amita, Krīḍita, Vikṣepa, Supriya, Rūpakānti! By the command of Vajreśvara, summon the yakṣas and yakṣiṇīs! Hūṃ avara 2 vattali 2 bhakṣa priye yogiṇīmadhye hūṃ 3 phuṃ svāhā!
Having repeated this, one should form a firm fist with the left hand and press it firmly against the region of the heart;
this is the mudrā.
Oṃ, O Lord of Wealth, Vattali Phruṃ, svāhā!
Having gratified [the deity] with this mantra, one should dismiss them. Thus ends the yakṣa-bali offering.

Again, standing in the same manner facing south, having established a triangular mandala with the *vajrapada* [step] upon a mountain of blood, and having scattered red flowers and presented the offerings, one should set down in a vessel made of well-baked *jambūli* wood—filled with dried and fresh fish, meat, onions, garlic, sesame flour, the five nectars (*pañcasudhā*), and various kinds of food and drink—and having summoned [the deity] by means of the previously mentioned mantra and mudrā for invocation, one should likewise touch the vessel.
Oṃ! Whether at a solitary tree, in a cremation ground, on a mountain, in a cave, or in a grotto;
by the side of a village, on a path, in a field, or especially in an empty house;
in a vessel, on dry land, or upon the earth—Mātanga is especially present there.
[One should worship] Kṛṣṇarudra, Mahārudra, and Devadatta who is well-supported; [as well as] Kṛṣṇa, Karāla, Bhībhatsa, and Vināyaka who has transcended Nanda.
Cāmuṇḍī, Ghorī, Bībhatsī, and Umādevī are indeed the sources of manifestation.
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā,
Bhadrakālī, Mahākālī, and Sthūlakālī are the Yoginīs.
Indrī, Candrī, Ghorī, Duṣṭī, Lambakī, Tṛdaśeśvarī, Kambojī, Dīpī, and Cūṣiṇī are the yoginīs residing in the villages;
they are of terrible form, of great form, and of fanged form, O Kapālin.
Wearing a garland of skulls, adorned with a necklace, possessing the great supernatural power of the khaṭvāṅga staff;
holding a sword and an axe in hand, likewise a vajra in hand and a bow;
O Great Bliss, Great Vajra, accomplisher of all desires and aims!
The great king of the yoga-maṇḍala, the lord of the vajra, the sovereign; likewise.

The Tathāgata of the Great Body, the stainless one who creates through yoga— this is the great command of the All-Pervading One. Oṃ kakka kaḍhḍhaṇaḥ babba bandhanaḥ khakkha khādanaḥ hūṃ 3 phaṭ 3 jraṃ svāhā.
Having repeated this,
one should form two vajra-fists and join them back-to-back.
With the *toṣaṇamudrā* bound— [the mudrā] which has the earth as its canopy, is encircled by lotuses, is white, and consists of yellow pigment (*rocana*) and chains—
one recites: *oṃ tiṣṭha hūṃ, bhakṣa 2 jaḥ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having thus gratified [the deity], one should dismiss them.
"Whatever [offering] the yogin faces toward, he should cast right there"—this is the gathering of all bali offerings. This is the *bhūtabali*.
By this much, the *atiyoga* is also fully cultivated.

Furthermore, having meditated upon the yoga and the supreme yoga as being the nature of the unsurpassed worship of all Tathāgatas, one should fill a vessel made of mother-of-pearl or similar material with the five hooks and the five nectars; then, purifying it with fire, filling it with wind, flooding it with water, solidifying it with earth, and making it of one flavor with space, one should consecrate it twenty-one times—three times seven—with the mantra: *oṃ haṃ ho hrīḥ*.

Having removed the syllable *varṇa* by means of the syllable *ha*, and likewise the syllable *gandha* by means of *ho*, one should extract *vīrya* from the syllable *hrīḥ* by means of the conch of the Lord of Yogins. Again, through resolute conviction: Beholding the universal fragrance (*sarvagandha*), which has the nature of the splendor of the Lord of the Lotus family (*vanaja-jakulapati*) and is the banner of the Solar family (*mihirakula*), and which has the nature of the intellect of the Lord of the Vajra consisting of taste (*rasamayi-kuliśeśa-dhī-svabhāva*), one should transform it and cause the assemblies (*gaṇānām*) to be transformed. Having thus purified [the offerings] in this sequence, one should present them to all the Tathāgatas.

Furthermore, having purified [the substance] consisting of the beauty of nectar through the sequence of the five hooks and placed it in a lotus vessel, one should contemplate it upon the summit of Mount Meru—the crown of all existence—joined with the sun and moon and connected to all the limbs of the Sun and Moon. Having thus visualized it on this ground according to the intention of the Vivima, one should place the lotus of the Sun and, having churned it threefold with Meru, bestow the *cchiḍiṅga* many times according to the number of the Yoginīs.

Then, one should bathe the stūpa at the neck, which consists of the essence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-rasa*), by means of the falling of drops (*bindu*) for the gradual cleansing of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Having applied a drop to the forehead, the crown of the head, and the tip of the tongue—forming the "three dots" (*tripuṇḍra*)—one should recite this verse: "The Dharma is seen and purified; do not abandon its true nature. Whether Brahmin, dog, or outcaste, all are consumed within the single essence. Having recited this verse, while contemplating the oneness of the essence of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-rasa-ekatā*), one should partake [of the substance] and also honor others.

Others should also grasp [the practice] in the same way, beginning with the *kamalāvarta*. "Religious duty is priceless, free from the stains of passion; Avoiding the grasping of verses, bow down with a mind absorbed in reality. Having recited this verse which proclaims the ultimate truth, one whose consciousness is focused solely on the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) should cover the mouth and scatter [the offerings], while contemplating whatever desired action is to be performed upon the vessel for the *bali* offering.

Thus, the yogin—having been brought under control by the touch of the bliss of certainty born from the enjoyment of the splendor of the five hooks, the five nectars, and the ambrosia; having been gratified by the worship of the great passion of all the Tathāgatas; standing in the center of the wheel and maintaining the ego-identity of the Yogāmbara; with a mind colored by the ocean of great compassion—[unites] with his own consort, who has been cultivated through the previously mentioned sequence of the three unions, who bears the symbolic mudrās of the Jñānaḍākinīs, and whose intellect is dyed with great compassion.
Having visualized the great vajra emerging from the seed-syllables consisting of the five Buddhas,
one should place therein that which is fashioned from the three groups of three. First, having visualized the lotus of Kālī, which has the radiance of a *vaka* flower.
In the center of the parasol of desire, one should contemplate the two radiant syllables; from them,
the nectar born of the continuous flow of the movement of the series of rays gradually drips down through the eighteen channels.
Hūṃ!
O you who possess a harsh diamond-like heart, you who have swallowed [the world] alone;
O Umā, destroyer of the multitude of poisons and venom, may you break my body!
She who repeatedly destroys the mind-born god of love with her nails,
who is fierce and terrible, having abandoned [worldly ties], she is the subduer of Vaitālī.

Thus, having embraced her who was singing with limbs trembling from passion for Kauhuta, the yogi—his mind sluggish with the drowsiness of sleep born from attaining the causeless bliss of sporting with flowers and bees—filled intensely the seed-syllable within the flower of the ḍākinī, which is the means for all Tathāgatas to reach the world and the true nature of all phenomena. Having bound it and caused it to float upward, he should subsequently fashion the lunar disk (*indubimba*). Having placed the seed-syllable at the tip of the vajra there as well, shining with white light, he should consume it with Mount Sumeru along with the heroes who have ripened through their virtues. o ||
Thus, having brought face-to-face the equality of all phenomena through the delighted circle of ḍākinīs by means of this unsurpassed worship, he rings the bell.
HŪṂ 3 GHUṬU, HŪṂ 3 OṂ GHE 3 HŪṂ SVĀHĀ.
With this mantra of great satisfaction, one should satisfy [the deity].

Then, having visualized the mandala circle, one should fashion a rosary of beads according to the specific ritual action (*karma*), reflecting upon it with equanimity. In this regard, the characteristics of the rosary are as follows: for rites of pacification (*śāntika*), it should consist of crystal, pearl, mother-of-pearl, or any other white mineral substance, and should number one hundred beads. For rites of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), it should be made of gold, silver, copper, or lotus seeds, and should number one hundred and eight.

Saffron, red sandalwood, musk, realgar, and other coloring substances [should be used] for subjugation (*vaśya*). For malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), a *rudrākṣa*, *kālabīja*, or great conch shell measuring sixty [beads] is prescribed. However, in the practice of mantra (*mantrasādhana*), all [materials] measuring fifty [beads], or *putrajīva* fruit, are suitable for all rites (*sārvakarmika*).

Having taken up the beads of the desired measure as described in the section on the classification of ritual acts (*karmabheda*), one should wind a single thread around that seed nine times—using nine threads whose nature is like the sky (*yogāmbara*) produced from seeds such as *dhārāvarṣa* and others—and having knotted it together with that, the rosary is held within the hollow of the palms, which have been consecrated by the meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*) prescribed for the purification of the hands.
Having visualized that all the Arhat pills likewise consist of the qualities of the Buddha,
and that this which has the nature of the *dharmadhātu* is situated above Mount Meru.
The letter is the cause, the form is the purified essence of the seven; the number is the stainless, the unstruck sound, the essence of the yoginī once perfected.
Having thus gained conviction in reality by means of this verse on reality.
Oṃ, at every step may I become the Great Wisdom of all Buddhas; hūṃ 3 ho 3 a svāhā!

Having thus accomplished [the rite] with the sādhana-mantra: for pacification (śānti), a white support; for nourishment (pauṣṭika), a smoke-colored support; for winning affection (anurāgaṇa), a conch support; for malevolent rites (abhicāruka), a lotus support. Having drawn [the deity] forth with Vajrāṅkuśī, one should recite the mantra while counting [the beads]. This is the procedure for recitation (japavidhi). o ||

When one becomes weary from reciting [the mantra], one should bring the offering of leavings (*ucchiṣṭabali*). Having filled a vessel there with what remains after being consumed and drunk by the circle of heroes (*vīracakra*),
and having joined the two vajra-fists, one should apply white *arocana* to the corners of the mouth, raised up and formed in the shape of fangs.
Remaining established in this mudrā, one should recite.

Oṃ kuru 2 vattali mahāvattali siddhimukhi śmaśānavāsini pretamukhi caṇḍakarāli rudhirapriye samayārakṣite yogadhari, kili 2 rāve in the middle of the charnel ground, enjoy! devour! O messenger of the host of grahas, O smoke-colored one, O fierce Karālī, stay! accept! hūṃ! seize! seize! all the wicked ones! devour! devour! hoḥ phruṃ pheṃ phaṭ svāhā! Thus.
Then, having worshipped with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra) and given three snaps of the fingers,
one should likewise offer the bali mixed with food remnants at the four ancestral sites, on a mountain, at a tree, and again at a great river.
Thus ends the offering of the remnants.

Having thus presented the entire circle of heroes (*vīracakra*) as an offering, and having worshipped them as before with the *argha* and all other mantra-mudrā rites, preceded by the grasping of the vajra and bell, and at the conclusion of the praise beginning with "O Primordial Great Being," [he recites]: "Prostrate to the one liberated from existence; he who has no [other] refuge, whose limbs are beautiful. O Mother, grant the light of the embrace of the two, through your sovereign power! Hūṃ 3."

Having thus offered praise and dedicated the merit, and having placed the vajra-añjali at the heart preceded by the *kamalāvarta* gesture, and having performed the five-pointed prostration (*pañcamaṇḍalaka*) and the triple obeisance as before, one should remain in that same position and recite the verse of aspiration (*praṇidhigāthā*).
May all sentient beings be happy; may all sentient beings be free from illness.
Go by whichever path you may, and act so that you may attain Buddhahood!
I shall ferry across those who have not crossed over; I shall liberate those who are not liberated.
In the present age, I shall practice the yoga teachings.
Then, placing the *vajramuṣṭi* mudrā upon his heart, extending the *sūryakara* mudrā, and placing it upon the ground,
he should dismiss the supramundane deities while reciting "Oṃ gaccha svabhavanaṃ hūṃ saḥ svāhā," and afterwards dismiss the mundane ones.
Having recited the mantra "Oṃ, seize all malevolent beings! Go! For the sake of returning again! Hūṃ Phaṭ! and having snapped the fingers three times, one should dismiss them.

Then, having dissolved the pledge-maṇḍala into one’s own heart by means of the breath, and having performed the expulsion of obstacles, the eight-limbed prostration, the armor-visualization, and so forth as before, one should rise and dwell while performing the appropriate activities such as reading the scriptures, making offerings to the caityas, recitation, and fire-offerings. || o ||
The total number of this book, when carefully calculated, should be known as five hundred and fifty; it is neither less nor more than this. o ||
The one whose form is the ornament of the land of Nepal, who guards the view of the profound ocean of tantras,
and whose name consists of the auspicious words ending in "Varma."
Having diligently served the most venerable Guru,
the glorious *Catuḥpīṭha*— an auxiliary [text] described as having difficult-to-comprehend seals and its meaning concealed by the *Krama*— was taught.
Having heard the entire, well-concealed mantra and having properly understood the applications,
there is cessation through the attainment of true prosperity.
May the wise always wear this [work], which is bound together in a systematic sequence, around their necks like a yogic garment.

The Bodhisattva’s Ten Grounds Chapter One: The Ground of Joy Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great assembly of five thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats—free from outflows, free from taints, fully liberated in mind, and whose births had come to an end. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, there are ten grounds of the bodhisattvas. What are these ten? They are: the ground of joy, the ground of purity, the ground of radiance, the ground of brilliance, the ground of difficult-to-conquer, the ground of presence, the ground of far-reaching, the ground of immovability, the ground of good intelligence, and the ground of the cloud of dharma. These, Ānanda, are the ten grounds of the bodhisattvas. Then the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for a bodhisattva to enter the first ground, the ground of joy? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, it is because of ten causes and ten conditions that a bodhisattva enters the first ground, the ground of joy. What are these ten? Here, Ānanda, a bodhisattva has previously made vast offerings to the Tathāgatas; he has cultivated roots of goodness under many hundreds of thousands of buddhas; he has practiced the perfections with skillful means; he has been purified by the precepts of the noble ones; he has been protected by the Buddhas; he has been embraced by the Buddhas; he has been encouraged by the Buddhas; he has been praised by the Buddhas; he has been established in the lineage of the Buddhas; and he has attained the stage of non-retrogression. It is through these ten causes and ten conditions, Ānanda, that a bodhisattva enters the first ground, the ground of joy. “Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bodhisattva enters the first ground, the ground of joy, he attains ten qualities never before attained. What are these ten? He attains a body that is never again subject to birth; he attains a mind that is never again subject to affliction; he attains a speech that is never again subject to falsehood; he attains a resolve that is never again subject to wavering; he attains a power that is never again subject to defeat; he attains a wisdom that is never again subject to obstruction; he attains a vision that is never again subject to darkness; he attains a compassion that is never again subject to exhaustion; he attains a vow that is never again subject to interruption; and he attains a skillful means that is never again subject to regression. These, Ānanda, are the ten qualities never before attained that a bodhisattva attains upon entering the first ground, the ground of joy. [The text continues with the detailed description of the ten stages. Chapter Ten: The Ground of the Cloud of Dharma “Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells on the tenth ground, the ground of the cloud of dharma, he is like the great king of mountains, Sumeru, which stands firm and unmoving in the midst of the great ocean. Just as the light of the sun and moon cannot reach the depths of the great ocean, so too, Ānanda, no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can fathom the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the tenth ground. At that time, the Blessed One uttered this verse: ‘Just as the great ocean is deep and vast, And the sun and moon cannot illuminate its depths, So too the wisdom of the bodhisattva on the tenth ground Is unfathomable to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. The Blessed One having thus spoken, the venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly, including the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, rejoiced and praised the words of the Blessed One. Thus ends the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the first part of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

[2] By means of the opening, which is the cause for liberating all sentient beings through the radiation of non-duality with all Tathāgatas and the teaching of the Dharma, one should satisfy all the deities within their channels by means of the rays of light that have emerged in the form of the syllable *amṛta*. By means of the syllable *hrīḥ* from those rays, there is a lotus at the heart; at the throat, there is a five-fold stūpa. By means of the syllable *hūṃ* emerging together with the rays, one should cause the lotus at the heart to blossom. By means of the syllable *a* from those rays, upon a moon mandala, there is the syllable *hūṃ*, arising from wisdom and skillful means.

From the five things to be done for the benefit [of others], one should cause a manifestation in the form of atoms as numerous as the dust motes in all world-systems. Then, from two seed-syllables, there arises the Form [deity]. He has a smiling face representing white and yellow Wisdom and Means; he is adorned with a crown of the two and five Buddhas, and is beautified by garments of silk and ornaments of all kinds of jewels. As for Jñāna, however, from two [syllables] accompanied by a vajra and vajra-bell, there arises a chain embracing [the deity] with the two arms of Wisdom, reaching across the back of the neck of Jñāna.

Thus, with those two [deities] having become all tastes and accompanied by the form of a lion, one should satisfy all the channels (*nāḍī*). Its very form consists of the seed-syllable accompanied by the rays of the nectar-vajra located in the heart. One’s own insignia, the syllable *HŪṂ*, is situated in front, joined with the vessel of the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*). It is white, yellow, red, and black, positioned respectively in the east, north, west, and south according to their sequence. Those seed-syllables are: *SUṂ KṢUṂ YUṂ HŪṂ*. Having meditated upon the four Ḍākinīs and the seed-syllables.

In the four corners of that variegated [mandala], starting from the northeast (īśāna), are the lion, tiger, jackal, and wolf, with their respective symbols and seed-syllables: *smryuṃ*, *hmryuṃ*, *ymryuṃ*, and *kṣmryuṃ*, in due order. [The deities hold] a noose in the left hand and a goad in the right. One should agitate the nectar (*amṛta*) through the non-dual yoga of that mandala of deities. Having visualized [the ocean] upon the salt-water ocean, one should look at it with the syllable *suṃ*; by this, a stream of salt-water nectar flows. Or, looking with the left eye at the syllable *a*, a stream of milk-water flows.

One should visualize the two fangs, the tip of the tongue, the tongue, the belly, the forehead, the head, the two nostrils, the two ears, and the back of the neck as all being a single stream of food. [The deity] has a stupa for a head; [one should offer] the supreme nectar of the syllable *HŪṂ*. One should bathe and meditate upon [the deity]. Then, drawn in through all the channels (*nāḍī*) within the body, it dissolves into the crown of the head via the hanging [channels]. With that nine-fold stream of nectar, one should satisfy the deities of the mandala in his heart by means of the *Umbā* [mudrā].

Through the intrinsic nature of that yoga, the yoga of the vajra and bell makes known the single abode-vajra, the *amṛtabindu-dharmadhātu*. Its established hand-placement (*karanyāsa*) consists of white and other colors on the right hand, and yellow orpiment (*rocanā*) and others on the left. One should perform the eight-limbed placement (*aṣṭāṅganyāsa*): *haṃ* yellow on the head; *hūṃ* black on the two eyes; *yuṃ* red on the nose and ears; *suṃ* white on the tip of the tongue; *smryuṃ* white-yellow on the neck; *ymryuṃ* black-red on the two thighs; and *hmryuṃ* red-yellow at the navel.

One should visualize [the deity] adorned with a universal blaze, according to the specific ritual action. One should perform self-protection by means of the syllable *HŪṂ*. Within that, again within that, in the heart, on the back of the neck, and on the forehead, one satisfies [the deities] by hanging down a fillet at the end with the *samatālayā* [mantra]. All phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature. All phenomena are pure as a vajra; I am pure as a vajra. All phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga.

Having recited [the mantra] three times, one should press the palms together at the heart center. In a place agreeable to the mind, having spread out a canopy and raised banners and flags adorned with various hanging cloths and beautified by a network of tinkling bells; likewise, with fragrant mandalas in eight locations on all sides, and having placed the hand palm-upward, one should strike the summit of Mount Meru with the syllables *oṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
[3] Oṃ hūṃ svāhā. Having joined Śvetā with gnosis, the flower mudrā is performed. Oṃ śriṃ svāhā.

Having contracted the conch and lotus [gestures], one should employ the incense mudrā: *oṃ aṃ svāhā*. With the thumb raised as the gesture of gnosis, one should employ the lamp mudrā: *oṃ kṣuṃ svāhā*.
Placing the thumb in the center of the upturned palms like the sun and moon,
one should cause offerings of food, bali, and other items to be presented before the maṇḍala.

Oṃ iṃ svāhā. Then, having rotated the lotus, one should place the vajra-añjali at the heart. One should pay homage to the deities with the five maṇḍalas, with a mind intent on worship: "Oṃ, homage to you, hūṃ; I bow, hūṃ; homage, homage, hūṃ. In this way the deities are satisfied, and one should perform the triple prostration: "Oṃ, I offer myself for the service of the worship of the five ḍākinīs. Oṃ, I offer myself for the service of the worship of the Ācārya. Oṃ, I offer myself for the protection of all sentient beings. You are the pledge, samaya hoḥ, hoḥ, hoḥ."
I go for refuge forever to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
indeed, to all the three vehicles, and to the Yogaguhyā and the Ḍākinīs.
O Vīra, O Vīreśvarī Devī, O Bodhisattvas of great renown,
I go for refuge eternally, and especially to the Ācārya.

May all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, headed by Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Lokeśvara, and Amoghasiddhi, attend to me! I, [name], from this moment until I sit upon the seat of enlightenment, [take refuge].
I generate the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening,
just as the Protectors of the three times have made their firm resolve for perfect enlightenment.

I firmly undertake the threefold training in ethical discipline: the discipline of virtuous conduct, the discipline of gathering wholesome qualities, and the discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
From this day forward, I shall undertake the vow born of the yoga of the Buddha, toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha— the supreme and unsurpassed Three Jewels.
I accept the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā according to reality;
and I shall accept the master in the exalted assembly of the Great Vajra Family.
I shall bestow the four gifts six times every day,
during the delightful occasion of the Mahāratnakula yoga.
I receive the True Dharma— outer, secret, and belonging to the three vehicles—
within the pure Mahāpadma family, which gives birth to great awakening.
I truly accept the vow associated with all [the families],
performing acts of worship according to my ability within the exalted assembly of the great family of rites.
I generate the supreme, unsurpassed mind of enlightenment;
I have taken up the entire vow for the sake of all sentient beings.
"I shall cause those who have not crossed over to cross; I shall liberate those who are not liberated; I shall give rest to those who are weary; I shall establish sentient beings in nirvana."
Having first honored these Buddhas of the three times with devotion,
one should perform the confession of sins and so forth, as well as the rejoicing in merit.
Having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels, may I undertake all vows and follow the path shown by the sons of the former Victors.
Having cultivated the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), one should then commence the yoga:
sitting in the sattva-paryanka posture, holding the two hands upon the lap.
The tip of the meditative absorption is performed by extending [the hands] like the moon and sun,
blazing intensely in the ten directions with a brilliance equal to the fire at the end of an aeon.
The practitioner of Ghorī should place the seed-syllable *kṣuṃ* at the heart, which has the brilliant luster of fire;
by means of it, having addressed all men, she forms a resolve of no small contemplation.
Through the visualization of the mantra, there is the purification of the three realms:
*oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho ’ham*.
Cultivation in the absence of existence is existence; cultivation is not at all existence.
Thus, existence would not be existence. [End of 3]
